stem: Which principle best explains why some vaccines are given in repeat doses rather than as closely spaced doses over a few days?

options.text: Spacing allows time for immune memory development
Spacing is needed so maternal IgG can become an adjuvant
Spacing prevents all adverse events following immunisation
Spacing converts a non-replicating vaccine into a live vaccine
Spacing is only used to reduce clinic workload

explanation: Spacing allows time for immune memory development. Repeat doses work best when there is enough time between them for the immune system to generate and strengthen memory responses, rather than giving doses too close together.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Immunisation; Adverse Events Following Immunisation (AEFI)

optionExplanations.A: Correct because appropriate spacing gives the immune system time to develop and strengthen memory responses after vaccination.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because maternal IgG can interfere with vaccine responses rather than act as an adjuvant.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because spacing does not prevent all adverse events following immunisation.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because spacing does not change a vaccine’s formulation or make a non-replicating vaccine live.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because the reason for spacing is immunological, not just to reduce clinic workload.
